title: Triple Sum Nearest a Target
statement:
You get an integer array nums and an integer target. Choose three values at three different positions and add them up.

Return the sum that is closest to target. If two sums are equally close (one below, one above), return the smaller one.

examples.why: The possible sums are 5, 12, 15 and 10. 5 is only 1 away.
5 (0 + 1 + 4) and 7 (0 + 3 + 4) are both 1 away. The tie goes to the smaller sum.
Every choice gives 6. The same value may be used more than once if it sits at different positions.

hints: Trying every triple works but is cubic. Fix one value and ask a smaller question about the other two.
With the array sorted and the first value fixed, two pointers at the ends of the rest can walk toward each other: a sum that is too small moves the left pointer, too large moves the right one.
Check every sum the pointers produce against the best so far, using the distance |sum − target| and the smaller-sum tie rule. Stop early if a sum hits the target exactly.

explain.intuition:
Sort the array. Fix the smallest of the three values at index i, then look for the best pair in the part to its right. With two pointers lo and hi at the ends of that part, the sum moves predictably: moving lo right makes it bigger, moving hi left makes it smaller.

If the current sum is below the target, every pair using the current lo with a smaller hi is even lower, so none of them can beat this one; dropping lo is safe. The mirror argument holds above the target. So for each i the pointers pass through the closest sum from below and the closest from above, and comparing each sum with the best so far finds the answer in O(n²).
steps: Sort nums. Start best with the sum of the first three values.
For each i from 0 to n − 3, set lo = i + 1, hi = n − 1.
While lo < hi: compute the sum. If it is closer than best, or equally close and smaller, update best.
If the sum equals target, return it. If it is smaller, move lo right; otherwise move hi left.
pitfalls: Starting best at 0 or at Infinity and returning it unchanged. Initialise it with a real triple.
Ignoring the tie rule. In the second example both 5 and 7 are 1 away, and only 5 is accepted.
Skipping equal values too eagerly. The same number at different positions may be used twice, as in [2, 2, 2, 2].

solutions.title: Every triple
solutions.idea: Three nested loops over positions i < j < k. Keep the closest sum, smaller on ties.

solutions.title: Sort, then two pointers per first value
solutions.idea: Fix the first value, then squeeze two pointers over the rest of the sorted array. Every sum they produce is a candidate.

followups: Count how many triples have a sum strictly below the target. Which part of the two-pointer loop changes?
Choose four values instead of three. What is the cost, and can you do better than O(n³)?
